subject: Medicine
summary: Rheumatic fever is an autoimmune inflammation of the heart, joints, skin, and nervous system that follows untreated Group A streptococcal throat infection, mainly in children. Prompt recognition using the Jones criteria and secondary prophylaxis prevent permanent heart damage.

sections.p: Acute rheumatic fever (ARF) is a post‑streptococcal immune reaction causing multi‑system inflammation. Diagnosis relies on the Jones criteria, which combine major and minor clinical findings with evidence of recent streptococcal infection.
b: Major: migratory polyarthritis, carditis, chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules.
Minor: fever, arthralgia, elevated ESR/CRP, prolonged PR interval.

t.b: Does the patient have recent streptococcal exposure? High titres support recent infection.

t.a: Throat culture or rapid antigen test
t.b: Is there a current streptococcal throat infection? Positive test confirms active infection; negative does not rule out prior infection.

sections.p: Severity is graded by cardiac involvement: mild (isolated valvulitis), moderate (murmur with heart failure signs), severe (heart failure, cardiogenic shock, or severe valvular regurgitation). Neurologic chorea is staged by functional impact.
b: Mild: no heart failure, normal ventricular function.
Moderate: mild heart failure, NYHA I‑II.
Severe: overt heart failure, NYHA III‑IV, or severe valve disease.

sections.p: The trigger is a recent Group A Streptococcus (GAS) pharyngitis, especially in settings with limited access to antibiotics. Other infections are rarely implicated.
b: Group A Streptococcus pharyngitis (most common).
Concurrent skin infection with GAS (rare).
In low‑resource settings, poor treatment adherence and crowded living conditions increase risk.

sections.p: Patients, usually 5‑15 years old, develop fever, migratory polyarthritis, and a new heart murmur. Skin findings (erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules) and neurologic chorea may appear days to weeks after the sore throat.
b: Migratory arthritis affecting large joints, resolves within weeks.
Carditis: new regurgitant murmur, pericardial rub, or heart failure.
Sydenham chorea: involuntary movements, emotional lability.

sections.p: Investigations confirm recent streptococcal infection, assess cardiac involvement, and rule out mimics.
b: ECG for PR prolongation, arrhythmias.
Echocardiography to detect valvulitis, regurgitation, or pericardial effusion.

t.b: Is there evidence of carditis? PR prolongation or arrhythmia suggests myocardial involvement.
What is the extent of valvular damage? Detects regurgitation, thickening, or reduced function.
Are inflammatory markers elevated? Supports active inflammation; normal does not exclude ARF.

sections.p: Uncontrolled carditis can rapidly progress to heart failure, severe mitral or aortic regurgitation, and permanent rheumatic heart disease.
b: Sudden dyspnea, pulmonary edema, or hypotension.
New or worsening murmur with signs of heart failure.
Severe chorea causing injury or inability to care for self.

sections.p: Treat the underlying infection, suppress inflammation, and protect the heart. Use anti‑inflammatory agents and secondary prophylaxis to prevent recurrence.
b: Penicillin (or amoxicillin) for 10 days to eradicate GAS; chosen for narrow spectrum and safety.
Aspirin (high‑dose) for anti‑inflammatory effect; avoids steroids unless severe carditis.
Corticosteroids for severe carditis or refractory inflammation; avoid if mild disease.
Heart failure therapy (diuretics, ACE‑inhibitors) when indicated.

sections.p: Long‑term secondary prophylaxis with monthly benzathine penicillin G prevents recurrence and progression to rheumatic heart disease. Follow cardiac status with periodic echocardiography.
b: Monthly benzathine penicillin G for at least 10 years or until age 21, whichever is longer.
Echocardiogram at 6 months, then yearly if valve disease persists.
Educate families about early treatment of sore throat.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic ARF include septic arthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, viral myocarditis, and systemic lupus erythematosus.
b: Septic arthritis: usually single joint, high fever, positive joint fluid culture.
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis: chronic, not linked to recent strep.
Viral myocarditis: lacks migratory arthritis and streptococcal evidence.

sections.p: Normal ASO titres can occur if the infection was > 8 weeks ago or if the patient is a poor antibody responder; a negative throat culture does not exclude prior infection.
b: ASO may be low in early infection; repeat testing after 2 weeks if suspicion remains.
CRP/ESR can be modestly raised in other inflammatory conditions.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden shortness of breath or chest pain
Rapidly worsening heart murmur with signs of heart failure
Severe chorea causing injury or inability to eat

faq.q: Why does a throat infection cause heart damage?
faq.a: Molecular mimicry makes antibodies against streptococcal antigens cross‑react with cardiac tissue, leading to inflammation.
No; only the streptococcal infection is contagious, not the autoimmune reaction.
It is rare but can occur, especially in those with untreated strep infections or poor access to care.

Describe the pathophysiology linking Group A streptococcal infection to cardiac involvement.
Outline the acute management of severe carditis in rheumatic fever.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Focused history and systematic exam reveal the classic Jones pattern and cardiac involvement while excluding mimics.
b: Onset of fever, joint pain or swelling, and any skin rash within 4 weeks of a sore throat or skin infection.
Exact sequence of joint involvement – migratory, large joints, each episode lasting < 3 days.
Presence of new cardiac murmur, chest pain, dyspnoea, palpitations, or pericardial rub.
Neurological symptoms – involuntary choreiform movements, emotional lability, or behavioural change.
Recent streptococcal exposure: throat pain, scarlet fever rash, or impetigo; any antibiotic taken.
Social factors: crowded living conditions, poor access to antibiotics, recent travel to endemic area.

t.b: Listen for new regurgitant murmurs (mitral or aortic); a holosystolic murmur at the apex suggests mitral regurgitation, a decrescendo diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge suggests aortic regurgitation. Absence of murmur does not rule out early carditis.

Inspect for swelling, warmth, and limited active motion; passive range should be full. Positive finding supports major arthritis. Bedside exam cannot grade severity of synovitis beyond presence/absence.

Observe for brief, irregular, non‑rhythmic movements of face, limbs, or trunk; ask patient to perform rapid alternating movements. Positive finding confirms Sydenham chorea. Bedside test cannot quantify antibody titres.
Look for erythema marginatum – evanescent, non‑pruritic, serpiginous rash with clear centre, usually on trunk or limbs. Presence supports major criterion. Absence does not exclude disease.

Check for raised jugular venous pressure, peripheral edema, hepatomegaly, and crackles. Positive signs indicate moderate or severe carditis. Bedside exam cannot differentiate primary valvular regurgitation from secondary volume overload.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Each test answers a specific diagnostic question; when unavailable, use clinical surrogates.
b: ECG – detects PR‑interval prolongation, atrial arrhythmias, or conduction block; a PR > 0.20 s supports minor criterion.
Echocardiography – visualises valve thickening, regurgitation, and pericardial effusion; colour Doppler showing mitral regurgitation jet > 2 cm² confirms major carditis.
ASO titre or anti‑DNAse B – evidence of recent streptococcal infection; a rise ≥ 200 Todd units (or ≥ 2‑fold rise) is positive.
Complete blood count – leukocytosis may be present; anaemia of chronic disease can develop in chronic rheumatic heart disease.

t.b: Answers: Is there conduction delay? A prolonged PR interval (>0.20 s) or first‑degree AV block confirms a minor Jones criterion. If ECG unavailable, rely on clinical signs of carditis.

Answers: What is the extent of valvular involvement? Detects regurgitant jets, leaflet thickening, and pericardial effusion. A regurgitant jet area ≥ 2 cm² or valve thickening > 3 mm meets major carditis. If echo unavailable, use auscultation plus clinical heart failure signs.
Answers: Is there recent GAS exposure? A titre ≥ 200 Todd units (or a 2‑fold rise in paired samples) is positive. If serology unavailable, use documented recent throat culture or rapid antigen test.

Answers: Is there pulmonary congestion or cardiomegaly? Enlarged cardiac silhouette or pulmonary oedema supports moderate/severe carditis. If X‑ray unavailable, assess for clinical signs of heart failure.

sections.p: Apply the 2015 revised Jones criteria; stage severity by cardiac involvement and functional status.
b: Diagnosis requires ≥ 2 major criteria or 1 major + ≥ 2 minor criteria plus evidence of recent GAS infection.
Major criteria: migratory polyarthritis, carditis, Sydenham chorea, erythema marginatum, sub‑cutaneous nodules.
Minor criteria: fever ≥ 38 °C, polyarthralgia, elevated CRP/ESR, prolonged PR interval.
Staging – Mild: isolated valvulitis, no heart failure, normal ventricular function.
Moderate: valvulitis with mild heart failure (NYHA I‑II) or mild ventricular dysfunction.
Severe: overt heart failure (NYHA III‑IV), severe valve regurgitation, or pericardial tamponade.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic ARF must be differentiated by history, exam, and targeted tests.

t.b: Points to it: hematuria, edema, low C3, recent skin infection. Separate by renal panel (proteinuria, low complement) and absence of migratory arthritis or carditis.
Points to it: photosensitive rash, oral ulcers, ANA positivity. Separate by ANA, anti‑dsDNA, and lack of streptococcal serology.
Points to it: mono‑articular, high fever, purulent joint aspirate. Separate by joint aspiration culture and lack of other Jones criteria.
Points to it: prolonged fever, conjunctival injection, mucosal changes, coronary aneurysm risk. Separate by age > 5 years, cervical lymphadenopathy, and coronary changes on echo.
Points to it: persistent bacteremia, new murmur, positive blood cultures. Separate by multiple blood cultures, embolic phenomena, and lack of recent streptococcal throat infection.

sections.p: A structured approach ensures rapid control of inflammation, eradication of streptococci and protection of the heart while monitoring for deterioration.
b: 1. Confirm recent GAS exposure; obtain throat swab or ASO/anti‑DNAse B if not already done.
2. Start anti‑inflammatory therapy immediately – aspirin or high‑dose NSAID (e.g., naproxen) to relieve arthritis and reduce carditis inflammation.
3. Begin antimicrobial therapy – intramuscular benzathine penicillin G or oral amoxicillin for 10 days to eradicate residual GAS.
4. Add a short course of corticosteroids if severe carditis (NYHA III‑IV) or refractory to NSAID.
5. Monitor vitals, heart failure signs, and repeat echocardiography within 48‑72 h; adjust therapy if worsening.
6. Escalate to intensive care for pulmonary edema, hypotension, or arrhythmia; arrange urgent cardiology referral.
7. Initiate secondary prophylaxis with monthly benzathine penicillin G after acute phase, continue for at least 10 years or until age 40, whichever is longer.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Awareness of adverse reactions and interactions prevents treatment interruption and avoids iatrogenic harm.
b: Aspirin – risk of gastrointestinal irritation, bleeding, and Reye syndrome in children under 12; give with food, consider proton‑pump inhibitor if ulcer risk high.
NSAIDs (naproxen) – can cause renal impairment and worsen hypertension; avoid in severe renal failure, monitor creatinine.
Corticosteroids – cause hyperglycaemia, mood change, infection risk; give stress‑dose steroids if adrenal suppression suspected, taper slowly.
Penicillin – rare anaphylaxis; if history of severe allergy, use erythromycin or azithromycin, but monitor for QT prolongation.
Macrolides – interact with drugs metabolised by CYP3A4 (e.g., some antiretrovirals); check medication list before prescribing.

sections.p: Early recognition of organ dysfunction guides timely referral to higher‑level care.
b: New or worsening murmur with signs of heart failure (tachypnoea, peripheral oedema, hepatomegaly) – urgent echocardiography and cardiology input.
Pulmonary oedema or severe dyspnoea – start oxygen, diuretics, and consider inotropic support; transfer to ICU.
Arrhythmias (e.g., atrial fibrillation, high‑grade AV block) – continuous ECG monitoring; treat per ACLS guidelines and refer.
Severe chorea causing injury or inability to eat – start low‑dose haloperidol or valproate; involve neurology.
Persistent fever >48 h despite NSAID and antibiotics – reassess for superimposed infection or drug resistance.

sections.p: Co‑morbidities can mask typical findings, alter laboratory values, and limit therapeutic options.
b: HIV – may blunt antibody titres (ASO) and increase risk of opportunistic infections; prefer benzathine penicillin G and monitor CD4 count.
Tuberculosis – chronic cough and fever can mimic ARF; obtain sputum microscopy and chest X‑ray; avoid NSAID excess if TB meningitis possible.
Malnutrition – reduces albumin, exaggerating oedema; use weight‑adjusted drug dosing and supplement protein.
Pregnancy – avoid aspirin >30 mg/day and corticosteroid high doses; use penicillin and consider low‑dose aspirin only if benefits outweigh fetal risk.
Diabetes – steroids raise glucose; monitor capillary glucose and adjust insulin accordingly.
Renal failure – NSAID contraindicated; use acetylsalicylic acid at lowest effective dose and monitor fluid balance.
Liver disease – avoid high‑dose aspirin; consider corticosteroids if carditis severe and liver function permits.

sections.p: Tailoring care to vulnerable populations maximises efficacy while minimising harm.
b: Children (5‑15 y) – prefer aspirin over NSAID for arthritis; avoid Reye syndrome by not giving aspirin if viral illness suspected; use weight‑based dosing.
Pregnant women – penicillin remains safe; limit aspirin to low dose; avoid teratogenic drugs; monitor fetal growth if steroids used.
Elderly – higher baseline cardiovascular risk; choose low‑dose aspirin or naproxen with gastro‑protection; monitor renal function closely.
People with HIV – ensure prophylactic penicillin does not interact with antiretrovirals; screen for opportunistic infections before steroids.

Low‑resource settings – use intramuscular benzathine penicillin G (single dose) when oral adherence doubtful; rely on clinical exam and bedside cardiac auscultation if echo unavailable; use point‑of‑care CRP/ESR as inflammation markers.

facts: Jones major criteria: migratory polyarthritis, carditis, Sydenham chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules.
Jones minor criteria: fever ≥38°C, polyarthralgia, elevated ESR/CRP, prolonged PR interval.
Carditis severity: mild (isolated valvulitis), moderate (murmur with NYHA I‑II), severe (NYHA III‑IV or heart failure).
Penicillin prophylaxis: intramuscular benzathine penicillin G every 3‑4 weeks for at least 10 years or until age 40.
Echocardiographic hallmark of acute carditis: new mitral regurgitation with thickened valve leaflets.
Sydenham chorea pathophysiology: anti‑neuronal antibodies cross‑react with basal ganglia (molecular mimicry).

mnemonics.t: J: Joint (migratory arthritis); O: Oropharyngeal evidence; N: Nodules; E: Erythema marginatum; S: Sydenham chorea – core major criteria.

vivas.q: Define acute rheumatic fever and its immunopathogenesis.
vivas.a: An autoimmune reaction 2‑4 weeks after GAS infection; molecular mimicry leads to cross‑reactive antibodies attacking heart, joints, skin, and CNS.

vivas.q: What is the most specific major Jones criterion for rheumatic fever?
vivas.a: Sydenham chorea, because it is rarely seen in other conditions and indicates CNS involvement.

vivas.q: Why is low C3 in post‑streptococcal glomerulonephritis mechanistically different from rheumatic fever?
vivas.a: GN is a complement‑mediated immune complex disease, whereas rheumatic fever is antibody‑mediated cellular inflammation without complement consumption.

vivas.q: Which valve is most commonly affected in chronic rheumatic heart disease?
vivas.a: Mitral valve, typically causing mitral regurgitation progressing to stenosis.

vivas.q: Which laboratory finding would most strongly support acute rheumatic fever in a girl with erythema marginatum?
vivas.a: Rising ASO titre or elevated anti‑DNAse B antibody.

vivas.q: Explain the pathophysiological mechanism of Sydenham's chorea.
vivas.a: Auto‑antibodies against basal ganglia neurons cause dysregulated dopamine transmission, producing involuntary movements.

vivas.q: What is the primary goal of long‑term penicillin prophylaxis after rheumatic fever?
vivas.a: Prevent recurrent GAS infection, which is the only proven way to stop progression to permanent valvular damage.

vivas.q: Describe the echocardiographic finding most characteristic of acute carditis.
vivas.a: New mitral regurgitation with thickened leaflets and possible aortic regurgitation; no pre‑existing lesions.

vivas.q: Which physical sign is most characteristic of pericarditis in acute rheumatic fever?
vivas.a: A pericardial friction rub heard best at the left lower sternal border, varying with respiration.

vivas.q: List the bedside steps to assess for carditis in a child with suspected ARF.
vivas.a: Inspect for cyanosis, palpate apex beat for displacement, auscultate for new murmurs (mitral/aortic regurgitation), assess for rub, check for signs of heart failure (rales, hepatomegaly, peripheral edema).

vivas.q: How would you differentiate rheumatic fever arthritis from septic arthritis at the bedside?
vivas.a: Rheumatic arthritis is migratory, non‑suppurative, resolves in weeks, and lacks joint effusion; septic arthritis presents with single hot, swollen joint, severe pain, and often systemic toxicity.

vivas.q: When is aspirin preferred over steroids in ARF management?
vivas.a: For mild‑moderate arthritis or carditis without heart failure; steroids are reserved for severe carditis or when aspirin is contraindicated.

vivas.q: What bedside test cannot reliably differentiate between acute and chronic rheumatic valvular disease?
vivas.a: Auscultation alone; both can produce murmurs, so echocardiography is required for chronic changes.

vivas.q: In a low‑resource setting without echocardiography, what is the next best step to confirm carditis?
vivas.a: Rely on clinical criteria: new murmur, pericardial rub, heart failure signs, and prolonged PR interval on ECG.

vivas.q: Why is prolonged PR interval considered a minor criterion?
vivas.a: It reflects atrioventricular nodal involvement but is non‑specific and may be seen in other conditions.

vivas.q: What are the contraindications to using high‑dose aspirin in ARF?
vivas.a: Active peptic ulcer disease, severe asthma, renal impairment, or known aspirin allergy.

mcqs.q: A 14‑year‑old girl presents with fever, migratory arthritis, and a new holosystolic murmur. Which of the following would most strongly confirm acute rheumatic fever?
mcqs.e: ASO titre rises 3‑5 weeks after infection and is a key evidence of recent GAS exposure.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a major Jones criterion?
mcqs.e: Prolonged PR interval is a minor criterion.

mcqs.q: A child with ARF develops severe mitral regurgitation and pulmonary edema. What is the immediate management priority?
o: Administer IV diuretics and afterload reduction
mcqs.e: Acute heart failure requires diuretics and afterload reduction before anti‑inflammatory therapy.

mcqs.q: Which valve lesion is most characteristic of chronic rheumatic heart disease on echocardiography?
mcqs.e: Mitral stenosis with thickened leaflets and commissural fusion is classic chronic rheumatic disease.

mcqs.q: Which of the following best explains why penicillin prophylaxis is continued for 10 years after the last ARF episode?
o: To eradicate residual GAS in the throat
Because valvular damage progresses only while infection recurs
mcqs.e: Re‑infection can trigger further immune attacks, worsening valvular disease.

cases.v: A 17‑year‑old female with a history of ARF 5 years ago now reports exertional dyspnea and palpitations. Examination reveals a loud opening snap followed by a diastolic rumble at the apex, and a displaced apical impulse.

qs.q: What chronic lesion does this represent?
qs.a: Mitral stenosis secondary to chronic rheumatic heart disease.
Mean mitral valve gradient ≥10 mmHg or valve area ≤1.5 cm².

qs.q: What secondary prophylaxis is still indicated?
qs.a: Continue benzathine penicillin G every 3‑4 weeks until age 40 or 10 years after last episode.

mistakes: Relying on a negative throat culture alone to exclude recent GAS infection; serology is required.
Prescribing steroids as first‑line for mild arthritis, ignoring aspirin which is safer and effective.
Confusing low C3 in post‑streptococcal GN with rheumatic fever; they have different immunopathology.
Assuming a new murmur always indicates chronic disease; acute regurgitation can appear early in ARF.
Skipping echocardiography when it is available, leading to missed subclinical carditis.
Stopping penicillin prophylaxis before the recommended 10‑year duration or age 40, increasing recurrence risk.
Using high‑dose aspirin in a child with asthma without checking for bronchospasm risk.
Failing to differentiate migratory arthritis of ARF from septic arthritis, resulting in missed surgical referral.
